system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2176-04-04 22:33:00 to 2176-04-07 11:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of COPD, chronic alcohol dependence, and tobacco use, was readmitted one day after leaving a prior hospitalization against medical advice. He presented with shortness of breath and acute intoxication. He was treated for COPD exacerbation with prednisone, azithromycin, and bronchodilators, and his oxygen levels improved to the mid-90s on room air. His right middle lobe collapse remained unchanged on chest X-ray. He received diazepam for alcohol withdrawal and was encouraged to attend AA. Hypertension was managed with amlodipine. He was discharged home with a short-term oxycodone prescription for his right olecranon fracture pain, instructions to follow up with orthopedics and physical therapy, and a nicotine patch prescription to aid smoking cessation. He left with improved respiratory status and a plan for outpatient care.
problems: Acute alcoholic intoxication in alcoholism, unspecified
Closed fracture of olecranon process of ulna

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. You're here because you were having thoughts of self-harm and were found to be intoxicated. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah... I was trying to get into detox, but they turned me away. I’ve been drinking a lot—whiskey, every day. I just can’t take the pain anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned pain—where is it coming from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My elbow, mostly. I broke it in a car accident a while back. Never got it fixed. And my chest sometimes, from all the coughing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll manage your pain. But first, we’re concerned about your alcohol withdrawal. You’ve had it before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had bad shakes before. That’s why I keep drinking—to avoid that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor you closely and give you medication to help with withdrawal. We also noticed you were a bit short of breath. Any cough or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had a cough for a few days. Sometimes I feel feverish.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to check a chest X-ray and start you on some breathing treatments. We also gave you some fluids and a vitamin infusion to help with the alcohol effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray showed some collapse in part of your right lung, but no pneumonia. We’re stopping the antibiotic we started in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t have an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks like your COPD acting up. We’ll keep you on your inhalers and add a new one, Flovent, to help reduce inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my elbow? I was supposed to have surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The orthopedic team saw you. The X-ray shows the fracture hasn’t healed. They wanted to schedule surgery today, but you refused after the nerve block.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was upset. They made me wait too long. But I do want it fixed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They rescheduled you for tomorrow morning. But you’ll need to stay NPO—nothing by mouth—after midnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. We’re getting you ready for your elbow surgery. Did you follow the NPO instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Well… someone told me I didn’t have to fast anymore, so I had coffee with cream this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That means we can’t do the surgery today. It’s a safety rule. But you can call the ortho clinic to reschedule as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Man… I really wanted to get it done. I’m sorry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s okay. The important thing is you’re safe. We’ll give you a prescription for pain and the number to call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did a CT scan of your face because you said you were punched recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, at the bar. My face feels lopsided.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan shows no new fractures. The changes are old, from your past injuries. Nothing needs surgery now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s just going to stay like this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it’s not dangerous. It’s just cosmetic. We’ll note it for your records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Your liver enzymes were high, which we expected from drinking, and your platelets are low—something we’ll need to follow up on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my liver damaged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned it could be starting. That’s another reason to cut back on alcohol. We can help you find a program that treats both pain and addiction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know… I lost my two sons this year. I’ve just been trying to numb it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m so sorry. That’s a lot to carry. The psychiatric team said your suicidal thoughts have passed, but you should follow up with counseling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. I just want to feel better physically first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure was high when you came in. We restarted your amlodipine, and it’s much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped taking it. I forget sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve prescribed it again. It’s important for your heart and kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your oxygen levels are stable, and you’re feeling more alert. We’re going to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Already? What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with your inhalers, amlodipine, oxycodone for pain, and diazepam for anxiety. But no alcohol with those—especially the diazepam.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the nicotine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing that to help you quit smoking. And please call orthopedics to reschedule your surgery. Take care of yourself, James.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us. If you feel the urge to drink or have thoughts of self-harm, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I don’t want to end up like this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good start. One step at a time.

summary.summary_paragraph: James, a 60-year-old man with a history of COPD, chronic alcohol dependence, tobacco use, and prior trauma, was admitted for alcohol withdrawal and suicidal ideation in the setting of acute intoxication. He reported using alcohol to cope with chronic pain from an old olecranon fracture and recent grief over the loss of his two sons. In the hospital, he was treated for alcohol withdrawal with diazepam and supportive care. A chest X-ray showed recurrent atelectasis but no pneumonia, leading to discontinuation of antibiotics and initiation of inhaled fluticasone for COPD management. Orthopedic surgery for his non-healing elbow fracture was planned but canceled twice—first due to patient refusal and then because he consumed coffee before the procedure. A CT scan of the face revealed only chronic facial fractures with no new injury. His hypertension was re-managed with amlodipine, and he was discharged home with prescriptions for pain, anxiety, and smoking cessation, along with instructions to follow up on his surgical and psychiatric care.
